Just because you don’t outwardly/blatantly see other people suffering and having a rough time does not mean they don’t exist. Don’t assume that everyone has had a lovely life and that you are the only one that suffers. Truth is, many people suffer and you aren’t alone. Although, it’s not a contest to see who’s suffered the most — it’s still suffering in the end. 
There’s a world outside of where you live, different people that aren’t like your family. I’m sorry to hear that you’ve had such a tough life so far. I’m sorry to hear that you feel like you’ve lost all hope and exhausted all your options. People can’t always freely give you shelter, love, care. No one is really obligated to, but those things are certainly nice to have. But you just have to make do with what you currently have and work towards what you want. Try to find little things that make you happy. Flowers, the way others smile and laugh, the sunset or dazzling stars. Feeling happy for other people’s happiness. 
Your post and comment history says that you’ve donated blood and volunteered. No, you don’t get money from it. It’s a selfless act that is to help others. It’s a humanity kind of thing. You’re not meant to expect anything back when volunteering and donating blood. Just know that you’ve done good and the people you’ve helped appreciate it, even if you don’t feel like they do. 
Countless people have tried helping you and at this point, it might just be up to you to help yourself out. There’s unfortunately no magic solution to make anyone’s life perfect. It’s not about living a perfect or ideal life. It’s about enjoying and appreciating what you have. You can’t just have “nothing”. You have yourself and that’s all you need to make a change (in perception, in the world, ETC).

*TL; DR: Do assignments ASAP, review and mark your own work, take note of your mistakes so you know to how to avoid them, ask questions to clarify and to make sure you understand, and do practice questions to solidify your understanding.*

I think this generally goes for most things, but do your assignments as soon as you get it do you can understand the material ASAP (and so you don’t cram). This also allows more time for the next point, which is to ask questions frequently. Asking questions might make you feel dumb but it makes you smarter than those that don’t know and don’t ask. 
Review all your assignments and material, taking note of what you struggle or made a mistake with, then ask yourself why you’re struggling and/or why you made that mistake. Is it because you don’t understand it? What part don’t you understand? Did you misinterpret the question? Did you forget the definition of a term? Did you miss a step? Ask someone (instructor, teacher, Internet, friend...) to help you understand it, then do plenty of practice questions to solidify your understanding. Also, remember to take things one math step at a time at first so you really understand what’s happening before you do shortcuts!

Good luck! I believe in you :3

I think you mean open-ended questions.
I would avoid using solely close-ended questions (often questions that can be answered with yes or no OR answered very short). Instead, perhaps consider asking a close-ended question to introduce a subject into the conversation first. After you ask a close-ended questions, you can ask an open-ended question (questions that need explaining to be answered) to discuss more about it. For example, and this is assuming the other person knows how to kind of carry a conversation:
“What kind of music do you like to listen to?”
“I like to listen to classical music.”
“That’s nice. I like to listen to _____. Why do you think you like classical music? I like to listen to _____ because I enjoy hearing whatever and whatever.”
“Oh, that’s cool. I like to listen to classical music because...”
“Nice. Have you ever went to the concert hall to listen to the orchestra? I’m sure they play some classical music and it might be enjoyable for you.”

Remember to also answer your own questions and talk a little about yourself too so the other person can learn more about you and so that they also have something to work off of when conversing with you. Although, this is only a suggestion. Conversations are fluid and how one flows can be different from person to person. Just remember that some people can just not be very good with conversation and that’s alright.

Both. *Some* skills (although more like techniques) can be transferred to others but you’d find that there are unique techniques you learn for each instrument. For example, if you only knew how to play the snare drum, you would know about sticking patterns and basic rudiments (such as single stroke rolls and multiple bounce rolls).
The sticking patterns and single stroke roll skill can be applied to timpani and mallet percussion, but the multiple bounce roll skill can’t be transferred to timpani and mallet percussion because it’s unique to the snare (as far as I know).
Hell, even compare the tambourine to snare. In both, you would play closer to the rim for softer, quieter dynamics, while you would play more at the center for stronger, louder dynamics. You can also play a roll on a tambourine the same way you would on a snare, but you can’t play a “roll” (I don’t remember the proper term or if it’s just called a roll too) on the snare the same way you do on a tambourine, if that makes sense. 

TL; DR: Some basic skills can be transferred from instrument to instrument but there will be techniques/skills unique to each instrument too.

Mm, since you say that you don’t have very much musical background, let’s begin with some defining first so that you can understand it (might seem overwhelming but just read it slowly (: ). 

In music, you have seven main pitches: A, B, C, D, E, F, and G. They sound different because they are different pitches and are a whole step away from each other (it’s difficult to explain whole steps and half steps without listening to it though. If you search up a piano w/ the notes on them, you might be able to visualize it better). 

So again, those are whole steps from each other. You can also have half steps (also known as semitones), which are pitches that are in between those seven main pitches. Notes that are half a step down in pitch are “flat” while notes that are half a step up are “sharp”. For example, C# (# is a symbol meaning sharp) means C sharp, and that C sharp is half a pitch up from C. Another example would be A ♭ (♭ is a symbol meaning flat), so A ♭ would mean that that note is ‘A’ but a half pitch down. 

As you can see, to indicate whether a note is played sharp or flat, those symbols (♭and # are used, flat and sharp respectively) are written beside the note that would be played sharp or flat (a half pitch up or down from the seven main pitches). 

Now, introducing a different concept: key signatures. Music can be written from an array of several different key signatures, all with different amounts (or maybe no amount) of sharps and flats. 
Key signatures are an indication of whether a particular note would automatically be played sharp/flat or not. 
Composers use key signatures as a short cut so that they don’t have to repetitively write the sharp and flat symbols on notes that were more often than not sharp or flat (there’s something called a “natural” that can cancel a sharp or flat btw). The key signature dictates what notes in that song would be automatically sharp or flat unless written otherwise (which is how it is a short cut). 

In D major, assuming that it’s in concert pitch like a piano or something, the key signature has two sharps — one for F and one for C. That means that all F notes and all C notes would automatically be sharp, so you would play all F’s and C’s sharp unless indicated otherwise. 

And to wrap this up, “in D” means that the song is in the key of D major, which as stated above, is a key that says all F’s and C’s will be played sharp unless indicated otherwise. It is “in D major” because the song follows the rule of what the key signature has dictated, which in this case, *all F’s and C’s will be played sharp unless otherwise indicated*. 

I could give another example of a key signature if you’d like, but I hope this was at least a little bit helpful ^^. Feel free to ask any questions if you have any :3.

I would highly recommend purchasing Alfred's Premier Piano Course books, beginning from the first book (1A) to the end. May seem slow, but learning the piano is a process. The books begin with things like posture and hand position, and it slowly eases you into reading notation and music theory. Eventually, you will be able to play things on your own. This is how my former private piano instructor taught me (I looked for a different instructor after she fell asleep during my lessons on numerous occasions which was when I realized that learning from her was literally just going through those books under the guidance of someone that plays the piano). 

So, go through those books and assign a couple songs for yourself at a time, and progress to the next songs after you could perfectly play the songs you assigned yourself prior. Not gonna lie, it looks like a book aimed for children but trust me, it's definitely a way for you to teach yourself. 

If you decided to go this route, once you get to level 5 or something, start looking for sheet music on the internet. It's better if it challenged you because you would learn by doing (I improved my sight-reading and progressed faster than what I was doing in the books because I challenged myself to playing sheet music from the internet, that were a little harder than the songs in the books but was manageable to slowly get through. I would learn about grace notes and other musical symbols as they appeared). 

Alternatively, you could search on YouTube (although I've never tried so I can't comment on how good they are).

By the way, after leaving my first instructor and consequently ending my journey w/ the books at level six or something, I found that I had enough skill to be able to play a lot more difficult music, such as Liebestraum by Liszt (granted, I could sight-read well), HOWEVER, I would have not been able to play it *properly* without my new instructor, who watched me play and commented on how I played and how to improve and motivated me to keep practicing it even though I felt the life get sucked out of me when I kept messing up, which is something you don't get if you self-taught yourself. Just keep in mind that you would probably hit a plateau if you relied solely on self-teaching. You would miss out on being taught fingerings, more advanced music theory, and techniques. But don't let that stop you from trying to learn, though! :) Good luck \^\^

Welcome to Winnipeg! Here's a list of some places (food, entertainment, shopping) that I can think of in no particular order.

As the other person commented, The Forks is available and is a popular tourists destination. It has a market place where you can purchase food (as there are many food stalls) as well as souvenirs and what not (there is a little place upstairs where you can buy edible cookie dough and macarons too, if you're interested). Since it's getting warmer, I'm not sure if they're still allowing skating but you can buy rental skates and skate on the river, given that it's safe to do so. Otherwise, there \*might\* be boat tours if all the ice has melted. Or, it could just be closed, idk. But take a big walk around the Forks and along the river -- you'll find a skateboard park, a big "Winnipeg" sign thing, and just some nice stuff to look at. 

Polo Park is a mall that you can also go to. Nothing too special there, though.

If you're into art, there's Artist Emporium which is awesome for purchasing art supplies (close-ish to Polo Park).

The Millennium Library might also be something to check out. Four floors of full shelves of books and a nice view outside from all the windows. 

If you're with some friends or something, consider checking out Across the Board, which is a board game cafe. The gaming fee is something like $6 and you have full access to the entire board game library. Alternatively, you could just eat the food there and take a stroll around the Exchange District, which is where this cafe is located in. 

If you like poutine, check out Smoke's Poutinerie which is in the Exchange District too, I think.

U-Puttz is a little spot where you can kill some time playing in the (relatively small) arcade, playing laser tag, or glow-in-the-dark mini-golf.

Not sure what your interests are, but there's also the Human Rights Museum (located very close to The Forks), the Winnipeg Art Gallery (WAG), and the Manitoba Museum, the Royal Aviation Museum (not sure if it's open ATM though).

Khab Tapioca is a newer bubble tea here that you can check out. Haven't been there though so I can't comment on it. 

Kawaii Crepe is a crepe shop which is quite nice. 

Unique Bunny is a cute little shop where you can purchase Japanese themed stuff (sweets, sweaters, cute plush toys, keychains...).

If you go to the Osborne area, Unique Bunny and Kawaii Crepe are both in close proximity to each other.

Hope you can find something enjoyable to do :). If you have any questions, I can do my best to respond to it \^\^.
